summary: The English of 2:1-2:6 is mostly faithful to the Hebrew and to Bartenura and Rambam. There are two errors of sense: 2:5 rendered וְלֹא כָל 'not everyone' as 'no one', and 2:4 closed Hillel's quotation in the wrong place. Most faults are in the word analysis: many tokens were tied to the wrong BDB homograph (Adam, Sacar, Mattan, Ain, Azem, Shem, Dan, 'where?' for אֵין, 'island' for אִי, 'menstruation' for עַד, 'children' for טוּף, a bird for רָאָה, 'horse' for פָּרַשׁ), and many senses were filled in mechanically (sense 1 of an entry, or header senses of הָיָה). These are moved to the right Jastrow entries in the pack, or the sense is removed where the pack has no right entry. Some commentary rulings were inexact: Rabbeinu Yonah on the three things, Rambam's own reading of the reckoning clauses in 2:1, and Bartenura's textual remark on שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ in 2:4, which shows the English follows his second reading, not his first. The morphology patches fix binyan (Piel מְקָרְבִין, Peal יְטוּפוּן), gender (מְסַיַּעְתָּן), state, roots (ברר, צוף, שום), the adverb הַרְבֵּה, the Nifal participle label, and the split of אֵיזוֹהִי.

patches.value: 'Glory' renders תִפְאֶרֶת in both parts; both normative commentators read the path as the middle one, which is a glory to the doer and to people. 'Upright' for יְשָׁרָה: 'straight, right'. The reckoning clauses follow Bartenura (what a commandment costs against its reward; the pleasure of a sin against what it costs); Rambam's reading is recorded in the apparatus. The three things: the eye, the ear and the book of deeds, as Rabbeinu Yonah counts them: he asks why three are named when on the plain reading they are one, and answers by dividing them into deeds, speech and memory.
patches.reason: Rabbeinu Yonah does not 'add that the three are one': he raises that as a difficulty and resolves it by counting them separately (eye: deeds; ear: speech; book: nothing is forgotten). The note also did not say whose reading of the reckoning clauses the English takes.

value.summary: Rabbeinu Yonah: the Holy One sees and knows all human deeds and remembers them as if written before Him. He asks why the mishnah counts three things when, read plainly, they are one (God knows all and repays); he answers that it is a likeness: as a man is ashamed to act or speak improperly before kings and sages, so he should think at all times that he stands before the Holy One; he then counts the three apart (2:1:8–9).

patches.reason: The old summary said the three things are one; that is the difficulty Rabbeinu Yonah raises, not his view. His answer bears on the English, which counts the eye, the ear and the book as three, so the relation is 'follows', not 'not-applicable'.

patches.value: Rambam: the upright path is the good actions, the middle traits, by which a person acquires a worthy disposition and good conduct with people; this is 'a glory to the doer and a glory to him from people'. Be as careful with a commandment thought light (rejoicing on a festival, learning the holy tongue) as with one known to be weighty, because the Torah states the punishments of the prohibitions in eight grades but not the reward of the positive commandments. He reads 'reckon the loss of a commandment against its reward' as inferring a positive commandment's reward from the penalty for neglecting it, and 'the reward of a transgression' as the reward for refraining from it, measured by its punishment.
patches.reason: The old summary left out Rambam's reading of the two reckoning clauses, which differs from Bartenura's and from the English: for him הֶפְסֵד מִצְוָה is the penalty for neglect, and שְׂכַר עֲבֵרָה the reward for abstaining.

value: Variants: Vilna reads שיבור (base שֶׁיָּבֹר), לעושה (base לְעוֹשֶׂיהָ; Vilna's form is singular 'its doer') and עבירה for עֲבֵרָה (2:1.36, 2:1.46): spelling only, except that the singular לעושה differs in number.

Rambam reads the reckoning clauses differently: הֶפְסֵד מִצְוָה is the penalty for neglecting a positive commandment, from which its reward is inferred (Sabbath rest, punished by stoning when broken, outweighs circumcision, punished by karet), and שְׂכַר עֲבֵרָה is the reward for refraining from a transgression, measured by its punishment. The English follows Bartenura: the cost of doing a commandment against its reward, the pleasure of a sin against its cost.
patches.reason: Where the normative commentators differ, the reading not adopted must be recorded; Rambam's reading of the reckoning clauses was not.

value: אֵיזוֹהִי is the Mishnaic interrogative 'which is it', agreeing with the feminine דֶרֶךְ.
The saying is built of parallel imperatives with וֶהֱוֵי: be careful (זָהִיר), be reckoning (מְחַשֵּׁב); then the closing triad, introduced by וְהִסְתַּכֵּל.
שֶׁיָּבֹר is a relative clause with a modal yiqtol: 'that a person should choose'; יָבֹר is from the geminate root ברר.
The last clause is a nominal series: 'an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and all your deeds written in a book': these are the three things.
patches.reason: Hebrew has no subjunctive; the yiqtol is modal. The root ברר is worth a learner's note.

patches.value: 'He' in the first saying is the speaker last named, Rabban Gamliel of 2:2. The suffix of רְצוֹנוֹ is God, per Bartenura. The saying of Hillel on 'a thing that cannot be heard' is ambiguous. The English, 'for in the end it will be heard', gives Bartenura's second reading: do not say a secret thinking no one can hear it, for in the end it will be heard. Bartenura says this reading goes with the base text's שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ. His first reading, which is Rambam's, goes with his lemma וְסוֹפוֹ: do not say what cannot be understood at first hearing. It is recorded in the apparatus.
patches.reason: The note said the English follows the first reading (words that cannot be understood at first). But 'for in the end it will be heard' is the second reading, the secret; Bartenura says that reading belongs to שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ, which is the base text. Nor was the other reading recorded anywhere.

value: Variants: Vilna reads תפרוש, תאמן and לשמוע (bases תִּפְרֹשׁ, תַּאֲמִין, לִשְׁמֹעַ): spelling only.

Bartenura's lemma reads וְסוֹפוֹ לְהִשָּׁמֵעַ for שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ לְהִשָּׁמַע. He says the reading שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ belongs to his second interpretation (a secret will in the end be heard), and that Rashi reads דָּבָר שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר לִשְׁמֹעַ, without אִי: do not say of a word of Torah that you can hear now that you will hear it later.
Bartenura's first reading, and Rambam's: do not say a thing that cannot be understood at first hearing, relying on the listener to understand it in the end after close study; people may misread it.
patches.reason: The textual variants named by Bartenura (וְסוֹפוֹ; Rashi's שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר) and the normative reading not adopted in the English were not recorded.

patches.value: Bartenura: do not make statements that cannot be understood at first, relying on the listener eventually understanding them, for people may err and become heretics through you; on this reading his text has וְסוֹפוֹ. Another reading: do not reveal a secret even when alone, saying no one will hear, for in the end it will be heard ('a bird of the air will carry the voice'); the text שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ fits this reading. Rashi reads שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר without אִי and applies it to Torah: do not put off hearing what you can hear now.

value: The second half of the mishnah is Aramaic: עַל דַּאֲטֵפְתְּ אַטְפוּךְ וְסוֹף מְטִיפַיִךְ יְטוּפוּן. The Aramaic relative דְּ replaces Hebrew שֶׁ.
The skull is feminine (גֻלְגֹּלֶת), so the speaker addresses it with the feminine suffixes -תְּ, -ךְ and -ַיִךְ.

The saying uses the root טוּף four times as a play: the Afel (causative) in אֲטֵפְתְּ 'you made float', אַטְפוּךְ 'they made you float' and מְטִיפַיִךְ 'those who made you float', then the Peal (simple) יְטוּפוּן 'they will float'.
אַף הוּא opens the mishnah as a link to the preceding sayings of Hillel.

verdicts.comment: Consistent on the upright path and on light and weighty commandments. On the reckoning clauses Rambam reads הֶפְסֵד מִצְוָה as the penalty for neglect and שְׂכַר עֲבֵרָה as the reward for refraining; the English follows Bartenura's reading, which Rambam does not share, so the two normative commentators differ and the English stands. The patches record Rambam's reading in the apparatus and the summary.
The English gives Bartenura's second reading, which he himself ties to the base text שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ.

Rambam's reading (speech that needs far-fetched interpretation) is Bartenura's first. But Bartenura says the base text שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ belongs to his second reading, the secret, and the English follows that. The normative commentators do not agree on one reading of this text, so the English stands; Rambam's reading is now recorded in the apparatus and its relation set to 'records'.
Consistent once 'no one who does much business' is corrected to 'not everyone': Bartenura says Torah is not found among those who go overseas, a limit on traders, not a denial of wisdom to all.
